title: SQL Joins & Set Operations: The Complete Handbook
summary: A dense, example-driven field guide to every SQL join type — inner, left, right, full, cross, and self — plus the set operators UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT. Covers matching semantics, NULL behavior, execution algorithms, cardinality traps, and the mistakes that silently corrupt result sets.

chapters.title: Why Joins Exist: Normalization & the Relational Model
points: A join is a binary operator: it takes two relations and produces one relation whose rows are combinations of input rows satisfying a predicate.
Normalization splits data to remove redundancy (customers separate from orders); joins are how you put it back together at read time.
Every join result is itself a table — that is why joins nest, chain, and appear inside subqueries and CTEs.
Relational algebra roots: cross product (×), selection (σ), projection (π). INNER JOIN = σ_predicate(A × B).
Foreign key = the declared link (orders.customer_id references customers.id); the join condition is the query-time use of that link.
A foreign key is not required to join — you can join on any comparable expression, including inequalities and computed values.
Vocabulary: 'left table' = the one written first / before the JOIN keyword; 'right table' = after. Order matters only for outer joins.
Join cardinality classes to name up front: 1:1, 1:many, many:1, many:many — misjudging this is the #1 source of row explosion.
Set operations (UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT) combine rows vertically; joins combine columns horizontally. Different axis, different tool.

chapters.title: The Running Example Schema
points: employees(emp_id, name, dept_id NULL, manager_id NULL, salary) — 6 rows, one employee has dept_id = NULL, one has manager_id = NULL (the CEO).
departments(dept_id, dept_name) — 4 rows, one department ('Legal') has no employees.
orders(order_id, customer_id, amount) and customers(cust_id, name) for the many-side examples.
CREATE TABLE employees (emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, dept_id INT REFERENCES departments(dept_id), manager_id INT REFERENCES employees(emp_id), salary NUMERIC);
Deliberate asymmetry: an orphan employee (no department) and a childless department (no employees) — these two rows expose the difference between every join type.
manager_id points back into employees — the self-join hook.
Baseline counts to memorize: employees = 6, departments = 4, matched pairs = 5. Every later result is compared against these numbers.
Rule of thumb used throughout: run the INNER JOIN first, then ask 'which rows did I lose?' — that loss is exactly what the outer joins recover.

chapters.title: CROSS JOIN: The Cartesian Product
points: CROSS JOIN produces every combination of left rows with right rows; no ON clause is allowed or needed.
SELECT * FROM employees CROSS JOIN departments; → 6 × 4 = 24 rows.
Result cardinality is exactly |A| × |B| — the only join whose row count is fully predictable without seeing the data.
Old comma syntax: FROM employees, departments is a cross join; adding WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id turns it into an inner join by filtering.
Every other join is conceptually a cross product followed by a filter — optimizers never actually materialize it, but the semantics are defined that way.
Legitimate uses: generating calendar × store grids, all size × color variants, filling missing combinations before a LEFT JOIN to real data.
Pattern — dense report scaffold: SELECT d.dept_name, m.month FROM departments d CROSS JOIN months m LEFT JOIN sales s ON ...
CROSS JOIN LATERAL / CROSS APPLY is different: the right side is a correlated subquery evaluated per left row (top-3-per-group pattern).
Accidental cross joins are the classic performance disaster: 100k × 100k = 10 billion rows. A forgotten ON clause looks identical to an intended CROSS JOIN.
Defensive habit: write CROSS JOIN explicitly when you mean it, so reviewers know it was not a mistake.

chapters.title: INNER JOIN: Matched Rows Only
points: INNER JOIN returns only rows where the ON predicate evaluates to TRUE for a pair of rows. UNKNOWN and FALSE are both discarded.
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name FROM employees e INNER JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id; → 5 rows.
Both unmatched rows disappear: the NULL-department employee and the empty 'Legal' department.
JOIN with no qualifier means INNER JOIN — the keyword INNER is optional and purely documentation.
Inner join is commutative (A JOIN B ≡ B JOIN A) and associative — the optimizer is free to reorder any chain of inner joins.
Row count is data-dependent: it can be less than, equal to, or far greater than either input. 1:many joins multiply the one side.
Duplicate keys on both sides multiply: 3 matching left rows × 2 matching right rows = 6 output rows for that key.
Non-equijoin example: ON s.amount BETWEEN b.min_amt AND b.max_amt — band/range joins are inner joins with an inequality predicate.
Multi-column join: ON a.tenant_id = b.tenant_id AND a.user_id = b.user_id — forgetting the tenant column is a classic multi-tenant data leak.
Use INNER JOIN when a missing match means the row is irrelevant to the question being asked.

chapters.title: LEFT OUTER JOIN: Keep Everything on the Left
points: LEFT JOIN returns all rows of the left table; unmatched left rows are padded with NULL in every right-table column.
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id; → 6 rows, one with dept_name = NULL.
OUTER is optional: LEFT JOIN ≡ LEFT OUTER JOIN.
Guarantee: output row count ≥ left table row count. It equals it only when every left row matches at most once.
A LEFT JOIN still multiplies when the right side has multiple matches — 'preserves all left rows' is not 'preserves left row count'.
Padding NULLs are indistinguishable from stored NULLs — COUNT(d.dept_id) counts only matched rows, COUNT(*) counts all.
Aggregation trap: SUM over a LEFT JOIN yields NULL, not 0, for unmatched groups — wrap with COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0).
LEFT JOIN is not commutative: A LEFT JOIN B ≠ B LEFT JOIN A. The preserved side changes.
Anti-join idiom: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL returns exactly the unmatched left rows.
Use LEFT JOIN when the left table is the subject of the report and the right table is optional enrichment.

chapters.title: RIGHT OUTER JOIN and Why It Is Rare
points: RIGHT JOIN preserves all rows of the right table, padding left columns with NULL.
SELECT e.name, d.dept_name FROM employees e RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id; → 6 rows, including 'Legal' with name = NULL.
Exact equivalence: A RIGHT JOIN B ON p ≡ B LEFT JOIN A ON p (same rows; column order in SELECT * differs).
Style convention: most teams forbid RIGHT JOIN and rewrite as LEFT JOIN, because reading top-to-bottom you expect the preserved table first.
RIGHT JOIN becomes genuinely confusing in 3+ table chains — the 'right side' is the whole accumulated join so far, not just the next table.
MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle all support RIGHT JOIN; SQLite historically did not (added in 3.39, 2022).
Legitimate niche: appending an optional dimension to a query whose FROM clause you must not reorder (generated SQL, ORM output).
Mixing LEFT and RIGHT in one query is a strong smell — usually the author wanted FULL OUTER JOIN.
Refactor drill: rewrite a RIGHT JOIN chain as LEFT JOINs and verify row counts match exactly.

chapters.title: FULL OUTER JOIN: Keep Both Sides
points: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched pairs, plus unmatched left rows padded right-NULL, plus unmatched right rows padded left-NULL.
On the sample data: 5 matched + 1 orphan employee + 1 empty department = 7 rows.
FULL JOIN is commutative in row content (column order aside), unlike LEFT and RIGHT.
Classification pattern: CASE WHEN a.k IS NULL THEN 'only in B' WHEN b.k IS NULL THEN 'only in A' ELSE 'both' END — the core of any reconciliation report.
Ambiguity: use COALESCE(a.key, b.key) AS key when selecting the join key, since either side may be the NULL-padded one.
MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN — emulate with (A LEFT JOIN B) UNION (A RIGHT JOIN B); UNION (not UNION ALL) dedupes the shared matched rows.
Safer MySQL emulation: A LEFT JOIN B UNION ALL (B LEFT JOIN A WHERE A.key IS NULL) — avoids UNION's cost and its collapsing of genuine duplicate rows.
Primary use cases: data migration reconciliation, comparing two snapshots, finding drift between source and target systems.
A FULL JOIN with a WHERE filter on either table's columns silently degrades to an inner-ish join — filter in the ON clause or wrap in a subquery.
FULL OUTER JOIN cannot usually use a nested-loop plan; engines typically pick hash or merge join.

chapters.title: SELF JOIN: One Table, Two Roles
points: A self join is any join where both sides are the same table; aliases are mandatory to disambiguate columns.
Manager lookup: SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;
LEFT (not INNER) is required to keep the CEO, whose manager_id is NULL.
Pair generation without duplicates: FROM employees a JOIN employees b ON a.dept_id = b.dept_id AND a.emp_id < b.emp_id — the < prevents both (x,y),(y,x) and self-pairs.
Using <> instead of < yields each pair twice; using = yields every row paired with itself.
Previous-row comparison: SELECT t.day, t.value - p.value FROM daily t LEFT JOIN daily p ON p.day = t.day - 1 — the pre-window-function idiom for deltas.
Modern alternative: LAG()/LEAD() window functions replace most self joins for adjacent-row logic and usually run faster (one pass, no second scan).
Hierarchy depth: a self join gives one level per join; N levels requires N joins — use a recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) for arbitrary depth.
Self joins on large tables can be expensive: the same table may be scanned twice unless the optimizer reuses a shared scan.
Gotcha: SELECT * on a self join produces duplicate column names — always project explicit aliased columns.

chapters.title: Join Syntax: ON vs USING vs NATURAL vs WHERE
points: ON accepts any boolean expression — equality, inequality, OR, function calls, multi-column conjunctions.
USING (dept_id) is shorthand for equality on same-named columns and merges them into a single output column.
With USING, the merged column is unqualified: SELECT dept_id (not e.dept_id) — and in an outer join it holds COALESCE of both sides.
NATURAL JOIN auto-joins on every same-named column pair. Avoid it: adding a created_at column to both tables silently changes the join predicate and breaks the query.
Old-style comma joins with WHERE conditions work for inner joins but cannot express outer joins portably; legacy (+) (Oracle) and *= (SQL Server) are deprecated.
Critical distinction: for INNER joins, a predicate in ON and the same predicate in WHERE give identical results.
For OUTER joins they differ: ON filters before padding (unmatched left rows still survive as NULLs); WHERE filters after padding (and NULL-padded rows fail most comparisons, killing the outer-ness).
Example — 'all employees, with their 2024 orders': ON o.emp_id = e.emp_id AND o.year = 2024 keeps orderless employees; moving the year test to WHERE drops them.
The one intentional WHERE-after-outer-join: WHERE right.key IS NULL, the anti-join filter.
Review heuristic: any WHERE predicate mentioning the right table of a LEFT JOIN is a bug until proven otherwise.

chapters.title: NULLs in Joins: Three-Valued Logic
points: NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE — so NULL keys never match, not even against each other.
Consequence: the employee with dept_id = NULL never joins to anything, in any join type, on an equality predicate.
Join predicates keep only TRUE rows; FALSE and UNKNOWN are both rejected. Outer joins then re-add rejected rows from the preserved side.
NULL-safe equality: a.k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.k (Postgres standard) or a.k <=> b.k (MySQL) treats NULL = NULL as TRUE.
Fallback for engines without a NULL-safe operator: ON (a.k = b.k OR (a.k IS NULL AND b.k IS NULL)) — correct, but usually blocks index use.
COALESCE(a.k, -1) = COALESCE(b.k, -1) is a common hack; it is only safe when the sentinel truly cannot occur in the data.
Distinguishing padded NULLs from real ones: join on a right-table NOT NULL column (typically its primary key) when testing for match.
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) after a LEFT JOIN: COUNT(*) counts padded rows, COUNT(right_col) does not — the standard 'zero-order customers' fix.
Set operators disagree with joins about NULL: UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT treat two NULLs as duplicates of each other.
Same for GROUP BY and DISTINCT — NULLs group together there but never match in a join. Memorize this asymmetry.

chapters.title: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins
points: A semi-join answers 'does a match exist?' and returns left rows once, never duplicating them — SQL has no SEMI JOIN keyword.
Semi-join forms: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.cust_id), or IN (SELECT ...), or a JOIN on a DISTINCT subquery.
Why it matters: a plain INNER JOIN to orders duplicates each customer per order — a bug when you only wanted 'customers who ordered'.
Anti-join forms: NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL, and NOT IN.
NOT IN is dangerous: if the subquery returns even one NULL, the entire result is empty, because x NOT IN (1, NULL) evaluates to UNKNOWN.
NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and generally the recommended default for anti-joins.
Performance: EXISTS can short-circuit on the first match; the LEFT JOIN / IS NULL form may materialize more rows, though most optimizers normalize all three to the same anti-join operator.
EXISTS ignores the subquery's SELECT list entirely — SELECT 1, SELECT *, SELECT 1/0 all behave identically.
Comparison row: INNER JOIN = 'matches, with multiplication'; SEMI = 'matches, no multiplication'; ANTI = 'non-matches only'.
Correlated NOT EXISTS is the canonical 'find gaps' query: products never ordered, users with no login, orphan foreign keys.

chapters.title: How Engines Execute Joins: The Three Algorithms
points: Nested loop join: for each outer row, probe the inner table. Cost ≈ O(N × M), or O(N × log M) with an index on the inner join key.
Nested loop wins when the outer side is tiny and the inner side has a selective index — the classic OLTP plan.
Hash join: build an in-memory hash table on the smaller (build) input, then stream the larger (probe) input against it. Cost ≈ O(N + M).
Hash join requires an equality predicate; it cannot serve ON a.x < b.y. It is the workhorse for large unindexed analytical joins.
Hash spill: if the build side exceeds the work memory budget, partitions spill to disk (grace hash join) and performance drops sharply.
Merge join (sort-merge): sort both inputs on the join key, then walk them in lockstep. Cost ≈ O(N log N + M log M), or O(N + M) if inputs already arrive sorted (index scan, clustered order).
Merge join handles inequality and range predicates and returns output already sorted — sometimes free for a downstream ORDER BY.
Outer joins are implemented as variants: the algorithm tracks whether each preserved-side row found a match and emits a NULL-padded row if not.
Full outer join is normally hash- or merge-based; a plain nested loop cannot easily emit unmatched right rows.
Reading a plan: look for 'Nested Loop', 'Hash Join', 'Merge Join' node names, plus estimated-vs-actual row counts — big divergence means bad statistics.
You do not choose the algorithm; you influence it via indexes, statistics freshness, and how selective your predicates are.

chapters.title: Join Order, Cardinality, and the Optimizer
points: The optimizer picks join order, not you — inner joins are associative and commutative, so any order is legal.
Search space is factorial: N tables have up to N! orderings, so planners use dynamic programming (small N) and heuristics or genetic search (large N).
Cardinality estimation drives everything: a wrong row estimate early cascades into a bad algorithm choice and a bad order downstream.
Selectivity estimates come from statistics — histograms, distinct-value counts, null fractions. Stale stats after a bulk load are a top cause of sudden slow joins.

Correlated columns break independence assumptions: city = 'Paris' AND country = 'France' is estimated as the product of two selectivities and badly underestimated. Fix with multi-column / extended statistics.
Rule of thumb: filter early, join late. Reduce row counts before they enter a join, not after.
Outer joins constrain reordering — the optimizer cannot freely commute them, so a long LEFT JOIN chain has fewer legal plans than an inner one.

Row explosion math: joining two 1:many relations to the same parent multiplies the children (10 orders × 5 addresses = 50 rows per customer) and corrupts SUM. Aggregate each branch in a subquery first.
Diagnosis workflow: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, compare estimated vs actual rows at each node, find the first node where they diverge by 10x or more.
Join hints exist (Oracle /*+ USE_HASH */, SQL Server OPTION(HASH JOIN), MySQL STRAIGHT_JOIN) but freeze the plan against future data change — a last resort.
Practical fixes before hints: refresh statistics, add the missing index, rewrite a correlated subquery as a join, or split a monster query into CTEs.

chapters.title: Chaining Multiple Joins
points: Joins evaluate left to right: A JOIN B JOIN C means (A JOIN B) JOIN C — C joins the composite result, not just B.
The 'left table' for the third join is everything accumulated so far — this is why RIGHT JOIN in a chain confuses readers.
One INNER JOIN anywhere after a LEFT JOIN can silently cancel the outer-ness, because the inner join drops the NULL-padded rows.
Fix: keep the chain LEFT all the way down, or parenthesize — A LEFT JOIN (B JOIN C ON ...) ON ... — to join B and C first.
Always alias tables in multi-join queries; unqualified column names become ambiguous and break on schema change.
Order the FROM clause to tell a story: driving/fact table first, dimensions after — readability, since the optimizer ignores your order for inner joins.
Fan trap: joining one parent to two independent child tables multiplies the children. Symptom is inflated SUM/COUNT. Fix by pre-aggregating each child in its own subquery or using a lateral join.
Chasm trap: two unrelated many:1 paths meet at a shared dimension, producing rows that correspond to no real fact.
Star schema pattern: one fact table LEFT JOINed to many dimension tables on their surrogate keys — each dimension join is many:1, so no multiplication.
Use CTEs to name intermediate results; a 9-table join becomes readable as three named 3-table steps with no change in semantics on most engines.
Sanity drill: after each added join, check the row count. If it changed unexpectedly, the newest join is many:many.

chapters.title: UNION and UNION ALL
points: UNION stacks the rows of two result sets vertically and removes duplicate rows across the whole combined set.
UNION ALL stacks them and keeps every row, including duplicates — no comparison work.
Requirements: both sides must have the same number of columns, in the same order, with compatible types. Column names come from the first SELECT.
UNION ALL is strictly faster: UNION needs a sort or hash pass to dedupe. Default to UNION ALL and use UNION only when dedupe is genuinely required.
Duplicate detection treats NULL as equal to NULL — the opposite of join predicate behavior.
ORDER BY applies to the whole result and must be written once, after the last SELECT, using output column names or positions.
LIMIT on a branch needs parentheses: (SELECT ... LIMIT 5) UNION ALL (SELECT ... LIMIT 5).
Common uses: merging monthly/sharded tables, adding a synthetic 'Total' row to a report, combining two different classifications of the same entity.
Type coercion pitfall: UNION of INT and TEXT columns either errors or silently coerces to text depending on the engine — cast explicitly.
Tag your branches — SELECT 'active' AS source, ... UNION ALL SELECT 'archived', ... — so you can tell where each row came from.
UNION is not a substitute for OR in a WHERE clause, but rewriting OR as UNION ALL sometimes lets each branch use its own index.

chapters.title: INTERSECT and EXCEPT
points: INTERSECT returns rows present in both result sets, deduplicated by default.
EXCEPT (Oracle spells it MINUS) returns rows in the first set that are not in the second, deduplicated by default.
Both compare entire rows — every projected column — not just a key column. This is the most common misuse.
EXCEPT is not commutative: A EXCEPT B ≠ B EXCEPT A. INTERSECT is commutative.
ALL variants (INTERSECT ALL, EXCEPT ALL) use multiset semantics: with 3 copies left and 1 right, INTERSECT ALL yields 1 and EXCEPT ALL yields 2. Supported in Postgres, not in MySQL or SQL Server.
NULLs match each other in these operators, so a row of all-NULLs in both sets is considered a duplicate.
Precedence: INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT; UNION and EXCEPT are left-associative. Parenthesize whenever you mix them.
MySQL added INTERSECT and EXCEPT in 8.0.31; before that, emulate with joins.
Reconciliation idiom for 'are these two tables identical?': (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A) — an empty result means they match.
EXCEPT silently collapses duplicates, so it can report 'identical' for tables with different row multiplicities — use EXCEPT ALL or compare counts too.
Practical use: INTERSECT for audience overlap (users in segment A and segment B), EXCEPT for churn (last month's users minus this month's).

chapters.title: Set Operations vs Joins: Choosing and Converting
points: Axis rule: joins widen (add columns), set operations lengthen (add rows). Pick by asking which direction the data grows.
INTERSECT ≈ a semi-join on all columns: A INTERSECT B ≡ SELECT DISTINCT a.* FROM A a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM B b WHERE b.* IS NOT DISTINCT FROM a.*).
EXCEPT ≈ an anti-join on all columns: rewrite as NOT EXISTS with NULL-safe comparisons on every column.
When you need only some columns compared, a join or EXISTS is correct and INTERSECT/EXCEPT is wrong — they always compare the full row.
Joins can multiply rows; INTERSECT and EXCEPT never do. That determinism is a reason to prefer them for set membership questions.
Set operations require matching column shape; joins do not. Shape mismatch is the fastest signal you reached for the wrong tool.
Performance: INTERSECT/EXCEPT typically sort or hash both inputs entirely; a correlated NOT EXISTS can use an index and stop early on the large side.
UNION ALL has no join equivalent at all — a FULL OUTER JOIN pads with NULLs into shared columns, it does not stack rows.
Comparison table to draw: operator | dedupes? | can multiply rows? | needs same shape? | NULL = NULL? — joins answer no/yes/no/no; set ops answer yes/no/yes/yes.
Decision flow: 'same entity, more attributes' → join. 'Same shape, more rows' → UNION ALL. 'Membership question' → EXISTS/NOT EXISTS, or INTERSECT/EXCEPT if whole rows are being compared.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and How to Catch Them
points: Filtering the right table in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN — turns it into an inner join. Move the predicate into ON.
Row explosion from a many:many join, then SUM over the inflated rows. Symptom: totals that are exact multiples of the truth. Fix: pre-aggregate.
SELECT COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN and calling it 'orders per customer' — it counts 1 for customers with zero orders. Use COUNT(o.order_id).
NOT IN against a subquery containing NULL returns zero rows. Use NOT EXISTS.
Missing a column in a composite join key — joins across tenants, dates, or currencies. Always join on the full key.
Trusting NATURAL JOIN, then adding an updated_at column to both tables and silently changing the predicate.
Using DISTINCT to paper over duplicate rows caused by a wrong join. DISTINCT hides the symptom and costs a sort; find the multiplying join instead.
Joining on a column wrapped in a function — ON UPPER(a.code) = b.code — which disables index use. Store normalized data or add a functional index.
Implicit type conversion in the ON clause (VARCHAR key = INT key) forces a cast per row and blocks index seeks.
Mixing UNION and EXCEPT without parentheses and getting left-associative evaluation you did not intend.
Verification habits: check row counts after every added join; compare against COUNT(DISTINCT primary_key); run the query with LIMIT on a known ID first.
Reconciliation habit: before shipping, run the old and new query through (A EXCEPT B) UNION ALL (B EXCEPT A) and confirm it is empty.

chapters.title: Performance Checklist
points: Index every foreign key column — the child side of a 1:many join is almost never indexed by default (MySQL/InnoDB is the exception).
Composite index column order must match the join predicate's leading columns to be usable for a seek.
A covering index (join key + selected columns) lets the engine skip the table lookup entirely.
Keep statistics fresh; run ANALYZE / UPDATE STATISTICS after bulk loads, or the planner will estimate against yesterday's data.
Push filters down: apply WHERE predicates before the join, not after, so fewer rows enter the join.
Select only needed columns — wide rows increase hash table size and make spills more likely.
Watch for hash spills to disk in the plan; raising work_mem / hash memory sometimes converts a slow join into a fast one with no query change.
Prefer EXISTS over IN for large subqueries with duplicates; EXISTS can short-circuit and avoids materializing the full list.
Replace repeated self joins for adjacent-row logic with window functions — one pass instead of N.
Batch/range joins on dates: an inequality join (BETWEEN) cannot use a hash join; ensure a sorted index exists for merge join or bound the range tightly.
For very large joins consider denormalization, materialized views, or partition-wise joins on the join key.
Measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, not EXPLAIN — estimated rows lie, actual rows do not.

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet & Mental Model
points: Decision tree: need only matches → INNER. Need all of table A → LEFT. Need all of B → LEFT with the tables swapped. Need both → FULL. Need all combinations → CROSS. Same table twice → SELF (alias it).
Row-count guarantees: CROSS = |A|×|B|; INNER = anywhere from 0 upward; LEFT ≥ |A|; FULL ≥ max(|A|,|B|); semi/anti ≤ |A|.
One-line semantics: INNER keeps intersections; LEFT keeps A plus intersections; FULL keeps everything; ANTI keeps A minus intersections.
ON vs WHERE, memorized: ON decides what matches; WHERE decides what survives. On outer joins those are different moments in time.
NULL rule, memorized: NULL never matches in a join, but NULL equals NULL in UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, GROUP BY, and DISTINCT.
Set operator quick table: UNION dedupes, UNION ALL does not, INTERSECT keeps common rows, EXCEPT subtracts — all compare whole rows and all require identical column shape.
Algorithms: nested loop for small-outer-plus-indexed-inner; hash for big equality joins; merge for pre-sorted or inequality-range inputs.
Debug ritual: run the INNER JOIN first, count rows, then widen to LEFT and see exactly which rows appeared. The delta names your unmatched data.
Reviewer red flags: a WHERE on a LEFT JOIN's right table, a NOT IN with a subquery, a NATURAL JOIN, a DISTINCT that appeared after a bug report, a join predicate wrapped in a function.
Default choices worth internalizing: UNION ALL over UNION, NOT EXISTS over NOT IN, LEFT over RIGHT, explicit CROSS JOIN over comma syntax, explicit ON over USING or NATURAL.
Final frame: a join is a filtered cross product plus an optional promise to preserve one or both sides. Everything in this handbook follows from that one sentence.
